source.title: Mitigating Memorization In Language Models
source.authors: Mansi Sakarvadia; A. Ajith; A. Khan; Nathaniel Hudson; Caleb Geniesse; Kyle Chard; Yao-Qing Yang; Ian T. Foster; Michael W. Mahoney

record.tranche_reason: The study uses localization-and-ablation unlearning methods, motivated by prior localization findings, and reports their memorization-mitigation performance. It does not test whether unlearned information can be recovered by the attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper measures memorized-sequence rates after unlearning and reports accuracy or perplexity as a preservation metric. It does not apply fine-tuning recovery, activation-direction restoration, quantization, or prompt-based attacks. Rows below record the reported post-unlearning memorization results, not evidence about recovery or attack resistance. Table results are selected best runs; Tables 1 and 2 are averaged over three seeds.
record.test_reason: The study builds and compares localization-and-ablation unlearning methods for verbatim memorization, and reports only how well each method mitigates and preserves performance. It never attacks the edited models: no relearning fine-tuning, no activation-direction ablation, no quantization, and no rephrasing or jailbreak prompts. So it cannot show whether removal is deep or shallow. Its measure is (n,k) verbatim regurgitation of injected noise or backdoor artifacts and of Pythia-extracted sequences, not targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that unlearning-based mitigation beats regularizers and fine-tuning in speed and effectiveness. They find BalancedSubnet best at removing memorized sequences while preserving accuracy or perplexity, and say methods developed on TinyMem transfer to Pythia 2.8B/6.9B.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates localization-and-ablation memorization mitigation (neuron and weight edits) on synthetic or Wikipedia artifacts and extracted Pythia sequences; it does not use the cited gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU setups and does not test recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by artifact type, model, unlearning method, and training point; the reported tables present selected best hyperparameter runs.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-unlearning verbatim memorization rates for TinyMem 4-layer math and language models (Tables 1-2) and for Pythia 2.8B/6.9B (Table 3). BalancedSubnet reaches 0.00-0.06% on TinyMem and 9.11%/6.53% on Pythia, with perplexity near baseline. Several methods leave language-backdoor memorization at 93-100%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Localization-and-ablation unlearning can cut verbatim regurgitation of memorized sequences while largely preserving perplexity or accuracy, with effectiveness depending on method and artifact type. Resistance to recovery attacks is not established.

record.problems: No recovery or attack-resistance test, so the results cannot distinguish deletion from access suppression. The reported tables select best hyperparameter runs; no uncertainty estimates are given beyond three-seed averaging for Tables 1 and 2.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the removed sequences. The study reports post-edit memorization and perplexity or accuracy only, and its measure is verbatim regurgitation, not knowledge accuracy near chance.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning. The FT rows in Tables 1-2 are fine-tuning used as a mitigation, not a recovery attack.
No direction ablation and no test of blocking access versus deletion. The loss-landscape figure (Fig. 4) concerns model health, not recoverability.
No quantization of the unlearned weights.
No rephrased, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context prompts. Memorization is tested only with the original prefix under greedy decoding.
BalancedSubnet is proposed as the best mitigation, but its resistance to any of the attacks above is never evaluated.

record.verdict_notes: All rows record the study's own method comparison, using best-hyperparameter runs selected by a memorization+perplexity score. They are not evidence on any version. The paper itself cites Shumailov et al. (2024): unlearned models can still be prompted to produce impermissible content. That is a cited result only, not tested here. Table 3 has no seed averaging, unlike Tables 1-2. Regularizer and fine-tuning-mitigation rows in Tables 1-2 were reasonably omitted, since they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover the targeted information; the paper reports post-unlearning memorization but does not attack edited models.
No ablation of an activation direction to restore information and no test of access-blocking versus deletion.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack.
No evaluation of resistance to the attacks listed in the claim.
